subject: parallel voter dispatch (card 237 retro pick, experiment)
result: PASSED round 1 (1 Yes, 5 Support-it, 0 No), confirmed by the independent re-run (3 Yes, 3 Support-it, 0 No)
seat_note: seats placed by card 226's decision-seat gate; all ran on Claude; the decider's first round-1 reply cited the proposal with one letter in a different case, so under D171 it was unread and re-asked once (counted: p237b-decider)

round1.reply:
Support-it

It meets the standing rules. Each voter runs in its own fresh context. There is a hypothesis, a metric (median minutes per window) and counter-metrics, and an accountability check that can FAIL a window. It is a two-way door with a 3-window scope, and the retro decides keep, revise or drop. It also targets a cost in the gate: windows went from about 3 minutes to 10 to 14. That speeds the path back to product value.

My reservation is that C1 to C7 specify a lot up front for one small change. The C5 serial fallback also makes the trial record murkier.

CITE: the number of voters and the quorum are unchanged

Support-it

P1: The change is minimal. It alters only when voters start, with no new file, seat or checker, and it is a two-way door.
P2: The accountability check is git-checkable: one window commit holding every seat-use line before the first voter result. The "within a few seconds" start-time test is fuzzy, so the auditor should apply it leniently to avoid false FAILs.
P3: C5 is the weak point. A collision on the shared seat-use history is only prevented by the launcher, so the serial fallback needs a clear trigger. It is recorded as a fallback rather than a pass, which is sound.
P4: The metric has a baseline, and D171 stays separate with no blur.

CITE: assigns the whole rotation up front, writes every seat-use line

Support-it

P1 (C1 to C3): The check is testable red first. A window launched serially, or with seat-use lines written after a voter started, shows up in git and in the votes file timestamps, so the check can fail it.
P2 (C5): "Cannot be made safe" has no test, so a parallel write collision could pass unnoticed.
P3 (metric): The median of 5 minutes or fewer is measurable. "Within a few seconds" has no number, which weakens the audit.
P4 (scope): Three windows is thin but fine for a two-way door.

CITE: all voters are launched at the same time, each in its own fresh context through the decision-seat gate

Support-it

Mostly verifiable from git. The accountability check relies on one window commit that holds every seat-use line and precedes the first voter result. It also relies on start times in the votes file.

Loopholes to watch:
- Start times are written by the facilitator, so they are self-reported and could be faked.
- A fallback to serial launch is recorded by the same facilitator who gains from it. The proposal doesn't say whether fallbacks count toward the 3 windows, so serial windows could be excluded from the trial.
- The median of 5 minutes or fewer could be reached by dropping slow windows.

The reviewer and auditor re-check should cover these. This is a reversible experiment, so it's worth running.

CITE: all voters are launched at the same time, each in its own fresh context

Support-it

Flow is my lens, and a vote window of 10–14 minutes against a 3-minute baseline is a clear flow cost. Parallel launch is the lowest-ceremony fix: it adds no file, seat or meeting. It is a two-way door, scoped to 3 windows, and it names a fallback to serial launch. The C5 write-collision risk on the shared seat-use history is real, but the fallback covers it. I'm not voting a full Yes because the accountability check, which needs start times within seconds, adds audit effort per window. Keep that check cheap.

CITE: parallel voter dispatch for every vote window

Yes

P1: The hypothesis is falsifiable. The baseline is measured per window on card 237, with card 234 and the pre-gate figure for comparison. The target is a median of 5 minutes or less.
P2: Counter-metrics (LRU violations, stale probes, unread votes, collisions, serial fallbacks) are named. Each is scored in its own record, so D171 and this pick do not blur.
P3: Sign-off is covered. The reviewer checks the window commit and the votes file's start times, and the auditor tick re-checks them. The trial retro decides keep, revise or drop by Decider.
P4: The change is a two-way door, and C5 makes a serial fallback count as a recorded fallback, not a pass.
P5: The scope is three windows, which is small, but the adopt/reshape/reject call still rests on recorded timestamps.

CITE: median minutes per vote window fall from 10 to 14

P2: The metric (median ≤5 min) and counter-metrics are measurable from git and the votes file.
P3: C5 is the weak spot. "Cannot be made safe → fallback" has no stated red test for concurrent seat-use writes. A fallback also must not count as a pass.

CITE: The facilitator assigns every voter of the window in least-recently-used order in one step

Support-it

P1 (C1, C2): The seat-use lines and skip records sit in one window commit, so git shows that they came before any voter result.
P2 (C3): The simultaneous start rests on votes-file timestamps. Git alone can't prove those, unless the file is committed and the launcher writes the start times itself.
P3 (C5): The serial fallback is self-reported, so a team could launch serially and call it parallel. The reviewer should cross-check commit times against the votes file.
P4: The median over only 3 windows is a thin sample, and the target is easy to reach by luck. The accountability rule ("counts as not run") closes the main loophole.
It is a two-way door, so I support it.

Yes

Vote windows cost about 10 to 14 minutes each since the gate, against about 3 before it. That is the largest flow cost on the line, and parallel launch is a thin, reversible change. It adds no file, seat or meeting. It reuses the existing commit step, and C5 falls back to serial launch if the shared seat-use history isn't safe. The 3-window trial and the single window commit keep ceremony small. Deferring the cap and preflight bundle follows the one-change-per-trial lesson.
